title.en: Food, the breaths, the senses and the body

summary: The Chamakam opens with a ṛk to Agni and Viṣṇu, which Sāyaṇa keeps apart as the mantra of a four-scoop offering; then begins the vasordhārā, the unbroken stream of ghee poured while all eleven anuvākas are recited, as the Kalpa he quotes prescribes. This first anuvāka asks for food and what goes with it, for voice, praise and hearing, for light and heaven, for the breaths, the mind and the senses, for strength, life and old age, and for the self, the body and all its parts. Every item is followed by ca me, ‘and for me’, and Sāyaṇa supplies to each the verb kalpatām, ‘may it be ready’, from the tenth anuvāka.

sandhi.rule: ā + i → e (ād guṇaḥ, P. 6.1.87)
visarga after ā is dropped before a voiced consonant (P. 8.3.17, 8.3.22): imāḥ vardhantu → imā vardhantu

samasa.meaning: Agni and Viṣṇu; in a dvandva of deities the first member ends in -ā (devatādvandve ca, P. 6.3.26), and the compound is dual

vyakarana.note: sajoṣas, ‘of one accord’, nom. du. with the Vedic ending -ā for -au. It carries its own accent, so it is not a vocative (a vocative inside the pāda would be unaccented). Sāyaṇa takes it as predicate and supplies भवेतम्, ‘may you be’.
Enclitic vām of yuṣmad, standing for the gen. du. yuvayoḥ or the acc. du. yuvām (P. 8.1.20). Sāyaṇa takes it as genitive with giraḥ: ‘your songs’, the praises addressed to you.
Vedic instr. pl. in -ebhiḥ, where classical Sanskrit has vājaiḥ; the Veda keeps the older ending (P. 7.1.10).
ā + gatam: gatam is the root aorist imperative 2nd du. active of gam (classical āgacchatam, Sāyaṇa’s gloss). The preverb is written with its verb.

translation.literal: O Agni and Viṣṇu, [be] of one accord; may these songs of you two grow; come with splendours, with vigours.
translation.readable: Agni and Viṣṇu, be of one accord. May these songs to you grow strong. Come to us with splendour and with strength.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa sets this ṛk apart from what follows. The Kalpa he quotes prescribes it for a four-scoop offering: «अग्नाविष्णू सजोषसेति चतुर्गृहीतं», after which the sacrificer fills a ladle of udumbara wood with ghee and, with ‘vājaś ca me prasavaś ca me’, pours the continuous stream of wealth, «संततां वसोर्धारां जुहोत्या मन्त्रसमापनात्», until the mantra is finished. That mantra runs through eleven anuvākas: «अत्र ह्येकादशभिर् अनुवाकैर्मन्त्रः समाप्यते». So he says of this verse «चतुर्गृहीतहोममन्त्रपाठस्तु» — this is the text for the four-scoop offering — and only after explaining it does he begin «अथैकादशानुवाकात्मको मन्त्र उच्यते». He explains the verse: Agni and Viṣṇu are to be of one accord (समानप्रीती भवेतम्); may these words of praise to you grow (वृद्धिं प्राप्नुवन्तु); and come here furnished with wealth and food (द्युम्नैर्धनैर्वाजेभिरन्नैश्च युक्तावागतमिहाऽऽगच्छतम्).

flags.note: vām may be genitive (‘your songs’, Sāyaṇa: युवयोः) or accusative, the object of vardhantu (‘may these songs strengthen you’), as Keith’s ‘gladden you’ takes it. The literal follows Sāyaṇa.

sandhi.rule: visarga before c becomes ś (P. 8.3.34, 8.4.40); so throughout: -aś ca, -iś ca, -uś ca

vyakarana.note: Enclitic me (for mama / mahyam, P. 8.1.22). The verb is not in this anuvāka: Sāyaṇa supplies कल्पताम् from anuvāka 10 to every item — ‘may [food] be ready for me’.
Every item is followed by ca me; the refrain is part of the text, not an abbreviation, and is recited with each item.

translation.literal: Food and for me, impulse and for me, effort and for me, continuance and for me, thought and for me, resolve and for me, sound and for me, hymn and for me, hearing and for me, what is heard and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May food be mine, and the impulse to act, and effort, and its continuance; may thought be mine, and resolve, and voice, and the hymn, and the power to hear and what is heard.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «वाजोऽन्नम्» — vāja is food. The word ca joins each item to the list (समुच्चयार्थः). मे means मम, ‘mine’, and the verb comes from the tenth anuvāka: «मे मम कल्पतामिति पदं दशमानुवाके वक्ष्यमाणं सर्वत्रानुषज्यते संपद्यतामित्यर्थः» — ‘may it be accomplished for me’. He reads the first six items around food: prasava is the sanction of food («प्रसवोऽन्नस्यानुज्ञानम्»), prayati purity (शुद्धिः), prasiti a binding, eagerness for food («बन्धनमन्नविषयकमौत्सुक्यम्»), dhīti the keeping of food («धीतिरन्नधारणम्»), kratu the sacrifice that produces food («क्रतुरन्नहेतुर्यज्ञः»). Then svara is the accent of the mantra (मन्त्रगत उदात्तादिः), śloka praise (स्तुतिः), śrāva the power to make others hear (श्रावयितृत्वसामर्थ्यम्) and śruti the power of hearing (श्रवणसामर्थ्यम्).

flags.note: prayati: Sāyaṇa glosses शुद्धिः, ‘purity’; Monier-Williams gives ‘offering, gift’ and ‘intention, effort’. prasiti: Sāyaṇa ‘a binding’, eagerness for food; the dictionary gives ‘extension, continuance’ (VS) among other senses. The word table gives the dictionary sense, the context Sāyaṇa’s.

words.gram: indecl. (used as a noun); the Taittirīya form of svar
words.context: Sāyaṇa: स्वर्गः, heaven
Sāyaṇa: one of the particular functions of the vital air (वायुवृत्तिविशेषाः)
Sāyaṇa: as prāṇa

words.meaning: the vital air vyāna, diffused through the body
words.context: Sāyaṇa: as prāṇa

sandhi.rule: visarga before c becomes ś (P. 8.3.34, 8.4.40)
final e before a: the a is elided into the e (pūrvarūpa, eṅaḥ padāntād ati, P. 6.1.109), marked by avagraha in the text
no sandhi across the pañcāśat mark: apānaḥ keeps its visarga before ca
as me’pānaḥ: me + asuḥ → me’suḥ

vyakarana.note: suvar is the Taittirīya form of svar, ‘heaven, light’, with the vowel the recitation inserts between s and v. It is indeclinable; its final r stands as visarga in pausa and becomes ś before ca.
asu, m., ‘life, breath’ (MW: from √as, ‘to be’), an old Vedic word; it follows the three named breaths.

translation.literal: Light and for me, heaven and for me, the prāṇa breath and for me, the apāna breath and for me, the vyāna breath and for me, life and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May light be mine, and heaven; may the breaths be mine, prāṇa, apāna and vyāna, and life itself.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: jyotis is brightness (प्रकाशः) and suvar heaven (स्वर्गः). Of the breaths he says «प्राणापानव्याना वायुवृत्तिविशेषाः» — prāṇa, apāna and vyāna are particular functions of the vital air. His gloss on asu is damaged in the printed bhāṣya (an editor’s note on the Kalpa’s ladle has run into it), and it is not reported here.

flags.note: Sāyaṇa’s gloss on asu cannot be read with certainty: the printed bhāṣya here runs together «असस्तद्वृत्तिमा» with a footnote on the Kalpa (‘व्याममात्रिम्’ should be read) and a stray «न्वायुः». It seems to call asu the air that has those functions, but this is not quoted or relied on.

with kalpatām, supplied from anuvāka 10: ‘may it be ready for me’

words.gram: n. nom. sg. (past participle of ā-√dhī)
words.meaning: what is thought upon; the object of thought
words.context: Sāyaṇa: the thing that knowledge always takes as its object (तेन ज्ञानेन सर्वदा विषयीकृतं द्रव्यम्)
Sāyaṇa: well known (प्रसिद्धाः)

sandhi.rule: final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23), written as the nasal of the following consonant's class (P. 8.4.59): m + c → ñc
final e before a vowel other than a becomes ay (P. 6.1.78) and the y is dropped (P. 8.3.19), leaving the hiatus: me ādhītam → ma ādhītam
final k stands unchanged before c
visarga before c becomes ś

vyakarana.note: ā-dhīta, past participle of ā-√dhī ‘to think upon’, used as a neuter noun: ‘the object of thought, anything intended or hoped for’ (MW, citing RV, VS, ŚBr).
vāc, f., nom. sg. vāk: the final c of the stem becomes k in pausa, and k stands before ca.

translation.literal: Thought and for me, the object of thought and for me, speech and for me, mind and for me, eye and for me, ear and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May thought be mine, and what thought dwells on; may speech be mine, and mind, and sight, and hearing.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: citta is knowledge produced by the mind («चित्तं मनोजन्यं»), and ādhīta is what that knowledge always takes as its object: «तेन ज्ञानेन सर्वदा विषयीकृतं द्रव्यम्». Of the four that follow he says only «वागादयश्चत्वारः प्रसिद्धाः» — speech and the rest, four, are well known.

flags.note: The printed bhāṣya’s lemma reads आधितं (short i) where the Saṃhitā has आधीतम्; his gloss on citta also ends in a misprint (ज्ञानय). The Saṃhitā is followed; the difference is noted, not resolved.

vyakarana.note: jarā, f., ‘old age’ (MW: the act of becoming old). As an item asked for, it is reaching old age; Sāyaṇa makes it the full length of life.
ojas, n. s-stem; nom. sg. ojaḥ, as sahas → sahaḥ and āyus → āyuḥ.

translation.literal: Skill and for me, strength and for me, vigour and for me, power and for me, life and for me, old age and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May skill be mine, and strength, and vigour, and the power to prevail; may life be mine, and old age.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: dakṣa is skill in the organs of knowledge («ज्ञानेन्द्रियगतं कौशलम्»), bala capacity in the organs of action; ojas is «बलहेतुरष्टमो धातुः», the eighth bodily constituent, the cause of strength; sahas is the power to overcome enemies («वैरिविषयमभिभवितृत्वम्»). Āyus he calls well known (प्रसिद्धम्). Jarā is asked for as the length of life: «जराऽऽयुषो वलीपलितादिपर्यन्तत्वम्» — life lasting until wrinkles and grey hair.
units.reflection: Old age stands in the list among things wished for, beside strength and vigour: to grow old is here a gift asked for, not a loss.

words.meaning: bodies; the parts of the body
words.context: Sāyaṇa: parts of the body not named before (पूर्वमनुक्ताः शरीरावयवाः)

sandhi.rule: visarga before c becomes ś
final a of the neuter n-stem (pausal śarma) stands before c
final e before a: the a is elided into the e (pūrvarūpa, eṅaḥ padāntād ati, P. 6.1.109), marked by avagraha in the text
as me’ṅgāni

vyakarana.note: Vedic nom. pl. of asthi ‘bone’ from the stem asthan, where classical Sanskrit has asthīni (MW cites P. 7.1.76). Kept as Vedic.

parus, n. ‘joint’, nom. pl. parūṃṣi: the s-stem takes a nasal and lengthens its vowel in the strong neuter plural, as havīṃṣi. The text writes the Taittirīya ँ before ṣ (परूँषि); the padaccheda uses anusvāra.
śarman and varman are neuter n-stems; the nom. sg. drops the n: śarma, varma.
tanū, f. ū-stem, nom. sg. tanūḥ.

translation.literal: The self and for me, the body and for me, shelter and for me, armour and for me, the limbs and for me, the bones and for me, the joints and for me, the bodies and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May the self be mine, and the body; shelter and armour; the limbs, the bones, the joints, and every part of the body.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes ātman in its highest sense: «आत्मा शास्त्रप्रसिद्धः परमात्मा», the supreme self known from the śāstra. Tanū is a body of fine build («शोभनसंनिवेशं वपुः»), śarman happiness (सुखम्), varman what guards the body, a coat of mail and the like («शरीररक्षकं कवचादि»). The limbs are to be whole («संपूर्णावयवाः»), the bones each in its place («यथास्थानं स्थितान्यस्थीनि»), the joints those of the fingers and the rest («अङ्गुल्यादिपर्वाणि»), and śarīrāṇi covers the parts of the body not named before: «पूर्वमनुक्ताः शरीरावयवाः».

flags.note: ātman: Sāyaṇa reads the supreme self (परमात्मा). In a list of the parts of the body the dictionaries also allow ‘the person or whole body considered as one, opposed to the separate members’ (MW, citing VS and ŚBr), and Keith gives ‘breath’. The word meaning keeps both; the context gives Sāyaṇa’s.
